title: Photocatalytic removal of textile wastewater-originated methylene blue and malachite green dyes using spent black tea ex

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states that sunlight causes excitation from a “valence shell to conduction band” and that the resulting “OH− radical” completely degrades dye. OH− is hydroxide ion, not the hydroxyl radical (•OH). Moreover, metallic Ag nanoparticles are not described by the conventional semiconductor valence-band/conduction-band electron-hole-pair mechanism asserted here. This is a chemically incorrect mechanism used to support the central photocatalysis claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Materials and methods: “Synthesis of SBT-AgNPs” versus “Optimization of parameters for AgNPs synthesis”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The basic synthesis says “1 ml of spent black tea extracts” was added to “9 ml of (100 mM) AgNO3.” In the optimization section, however, “1 ml of varying concentration ... AgNO3” is added to “9 ml of the prepared extract,” the reverse volume ratio. The final optimized preparation is again different: “2 ml of spent black tea biomass in 8 ml of 50 mM AgNO3.” These incompatible protocols make it unclear which reagent ratios and concentrations actually produced the characterized material.

The SBT sample is reported to have peaks at 38.3°, 40.8°, 64.5°, and 74.2°, assigned respectively to fcc Ag (111), (200), (220), and (311), while the paper itself reports the chemically synthesized Ag (200) peak at 44.3° and cites JCPDS 04-0783. For fcc metallic Ag with Cu Kα radiation, the (200) reflection is approximately 44.3°, not 40.8°; 40.8° cannot be assigned as the stated Ag (200) peak. Thus the reported SBT XRD position and its crystallographic assignment are inconsistent.

The manuscript says XRD was used “to study the particles size, dimensions and crystalline nature” and presents no peak widths, Scherrer calculation, instrumental-broadening correction, or numerical crystallite-size result. XRD supports phase assignment if the peaks are valid, but the manuscript does not provide the analysis required to claim particle size or dimensions from XRD.

predicted_errors.error_location: Materials and methods: “Applications coated-AgNPs for the removal of dyes”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The dye-removal experiment reports only 1 mL of a redispersed nanoparticle pellet added to 9 mL of dye/wastewater. It gives no catalyst mass, Ag concentration, nanoparticle concentration, catalyst-to-dye ratio, illuminated area, light intensity/spectrum, temperature, pH, or mixing conditions during the 180 min exposure. The nominal catalyst dose and irradiation conditions therefore cannot be reproduced or interpreted.

The stated comparison is a nanoparticle-containing tube under room light, a nanoparticle-containing tube in sunlight, and a freshly prepared solution “without SBT-AgNPs.” It does not clearly place the no-nanoparticle control under each identical illumination condition, and it has no dark catalyst control. Consequently, sunlight photolysis, adsorption of dye onto AgNPs/tea capping material, and apparent absorbance changes from nanoparticle scattering cannot be separated from photocatalysis.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and Introduction claims of “photocatalytic removal/degradation” and complete conversion to CO2 and H2O
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The reported analytical endpoint is UV–Vis absorbance decline. UV–Vis loss alone does not establish chemical degradation or mineralization: it may result from adsorption, aggregation/settling, photobleaching, spectral overlap, or scattering. No TOC/COD, chromatographic identification of products, mass balance, Ag leaching, or toxicity/product analysis is reported. The claims of dye degradation, non-toxic products, and complete conversion to CO2 and H2O are therefore unsupported.

predicted_errors.error_location: Materials and methods: identification and quantification of dyes in textile wastewater
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper identifies methylene blue and malachite green in an actual mixed textile wastewater by comparing UV–Vis “peaks pattern[s]” to prepared standards. Complex industrial wastewater has numerous overlapping chromophores, and no chromatographic/mass-spectrometric confirmation, calibration in the wastewater matrix, standard-addition analysis, or selective assay is described. Thus the method cannot validly attribute wastewater absorbance decreases or reported percentages specifically to MB and MG.

predicted_errors.error_location: Materials and methods: standard methylene-blue preparation and subsequent degradation experiment
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The standard-series procedure says 0.05 mg MB was dissolved in 10 mL water, which is 0.005 mg/mL (5 mg/L). The subsequent degradation experiment calls the standard MB concentration “0.05 mg/ml,” ten times higher (50 mg/L). This unresolved ten-fold concentration discrepancy affects calibration and degradation calculations.

predicted_errors.error_location: Materials and methods: textile-wastewater concentration and UV–Vis preparation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says “9 ml of (0.001 mg/ml) concentration of textile wastewater” was used. Wastewater is a mixture rather than a substance with a defined mass concentration, and no procedure explains what constituent was weighed/diluted to create this concentration. It also says “The concentrations of dyes (1 µl) were prepared and analyzed,” which is not a defined concentration or a usable spectrophotometric protocol. These descriptions prevent determination of what was actually measured.

The paper calls −17.5 mV “moderate colloidal stability due to high electrostatic repulsion” and says it prevents aggregation. In general, absolute zeta potentials around or above 30 mV are commonly used as the threshold for strong electrostatic colloidal stability; −17.5 mV is weak/moderate at best, not evidence of high repulsion or prevention of aggregation. The reported zeta deviations are also very large (10.8 and −13.7 mV), further weakening the stability conclusion.

The manuscript says EDX determined “purity” by reporting a strong Ag peak. A strong Ag peak only establishes that Ag is detected; it cannot establish sample purity without quantitative elemental composition, detection of non-Ag peaks, substrate/background handling, and appropriate standards. The purity claim is unsupported by the described evidence.

predicted_errors.error_location: Title and throughout: “spent black tea extract-coated silver nanoparticles”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The title identifies the product as extract-coated AgNPs, but the study provides no direct evidence of a coating or capping layer, such as FTIR/XPS/TGA, elemental mapping, ligand analysis, or comparison before/after washing. Negative zeta potential and inferred stabilization do not demonstrate a tea-extract coating. The material identity claimed in the title is therefore unsubstantiated.

predicted_errors.error_location: Materials and methods: “Chemical synthesis of AgNPs”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The chemical control is not reproducible because the trisodium-citrate concentration, total volume, stoichiometric ratio, and amount added are omitted; citrate is simply added “drop by drop until a color transition was observed.” Because this material is used for comparison in UV–Vis, XRD, SEM, particle size, and zeta potential, the uncontrolled comparator invalidates a meaningful green-versus-chemical synthesis comparison.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results: UV–Vis assignment for chemically synthesized AgNPs
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states that citrate-reduced chemically synthesized AgNPs showed their “characteristic peak at 310 nm.” The localized surface-plasmon band of citrate-stabilized Ag nanoparticles is ordinarily near 400–450 nm, whereas a 310 nm feature is not a characteristic AgNP plasmon peak. Without additional evidence, this assignment is likely erroneous and undermines the identity/comparison of the chemical-control material.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and dye-removal results as described in the abstract
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper reports precise removal values (25%, 58.3%, 33.3%, and 60%) and calls the results “remarkably significant,” but provides no replicate number, raw absorbances/concentrations, variance, error bars, statistical test, confidence interval, or p-value. “Significant” cannot be claimed from the reported single-percentage values.

The manuscript attributes to a “Pakistan Bureau of Statistics Report (2017)” the statement that “every Pakistani consume 15 kg of black tea annually.” This would imply several million tonnes of annual tea consumption for Pakistan’s population and is incompatible with widely reported national tea-import/consumption quantities (on the order of hundreds of thousands, not millions, of tonnes annually). The statement is also not supplied with a numbered reference or verifiable report citation and requires correction or a precise, checkable source.
